messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a 26-year-old detective who came to treatment months after leaving a violent marriage that, from the outside, had looked stable. He described repeated physical assaults by his wife that usually happened late at night after she had been drinking. What stays with him most sharply is not one single beating but the pattern: the sour smell of alcohol on her breath as she moved toward him, the moment he realized from her face that reason would not reach her, the blows, and the sounds that followed—her voice in a low, threatening tone, the slap of impact, his own breathing turning ragged. Because he works in law enforcement, he had felt especially humiliated by the abuse and deeply confused that he could read danger in strangers for a living but had not stopped it at home.

In the weeks after he moved out, the memories did not settle into the past. They remained vividly present, with an almost cinematic clarity that he found hard to explain. When they came, he did not just remember what happened; he sometimes heard it again in his head, especially her voice and the sound of being hit, as if the scene had broken back into the room. The memories forced themselves on him without warning. At work, if he interviewed an assault victim and noticed fresh bruising on a face or arms, an image of his wife standing over him would cut through his concentration. If a suspect or witness carried the smell of alcohol, the memory arrived even faster, complete and intrusive. At other times the trigger was in his own body: a wave of nausea would rise during a tense call or while driving home at night, and the nausea itself became a signal that the whole scene was about to flood back.

Those moments did more than bring back the assaults. They confirmed something Ethan had come to believe about the world. The sight of injuries on other people no longer registered simply as evidence in a case; it seemed to prove that people are not what they seem and that harm can be hidden inside ordinary intimacy. The smell of alcohol had become, in his mind, almost inseparable from betrayal. He said he had lost faith in people generally, not only in his former partner, and at times in life itself. Even around colleagues, he felt apart from everyone else, as though what had happened had marked him permanently and placed him outside the category of normal men.

That sense of being an outsider made the memories harder to contain. When he told himself that no one could really understand, the scenes returned with even greater force in private, vivid and unsolicited, as if his mind kept insisting on a reality he could not share. He was certain that people would either misread what had happened to him or quietly judge him for it, and this conviction left him alone with the sounds and images. The more he saw others as untrustworthy or fundamentally unreachable, the more the abuse seemed to remain immediate rather than over.

He responded by trying to shut down whatever might let those memories in. He stopped relaxing on purpose. If he noticed himself beginning to unwind at home, he would get up, pace, check locks, or turn back to work materials because letting his guard down felt dangerous. He also numbed himself emotionally; he spoke of moving through parts of the day flat and detached because feeling anything strongly seemed to open the door to hearing her voice again. Physical contact became especially difficult. When coworkers clapped him on the shoulder after a long shift or his wife’s replacement hand brushed his arm in casual affection—he is now separated, but not yet divorced, and still navigating contact from others—his body recoiled before he had time to think. Avoiding touch made sense to him because touch had become bound to the vividly recalled moments he could not control.

Over time these habits hardened his view of other people. Pulling away from touch, staying constantly braced, and numbing himself left him increasingly convinced that closeness was unsafe and that he did not belong with other people anymore. His marriage had ended, and he had become more isolated at work as well; other detectives noticed he lingered less in the bullpen and volunteered to handle tasks alone. The strategies that were supposed to protect him ended up reinforcing his belief that trust was a mistake.

They also narrowed his world in practical ways that kept him sensitized to the very cues he dreaded. Because he would not relax, his body stayed tense and easily unsettled, and nausea came on more readily during the day. Because he avoided ordinary contact, even small movements by others in crowded hallways or during field work felt abrupt and jolting, making him more alert to signs of injury, threat, and contamination. On one recent case he had to photograph a victim’s facial wounds while standing near an intoxicated witness, and he became so overwhelmed by nausea, the smell of alcohol, and the instant replay of the abuse in his mind that he had to step out and let a partner finish. That incident frightened him enough to seek help. He said he is afraid that if this continues he will lose his marriage completely, lose his footing as a detective, and remain permanently cut off from other people. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget, but to be able to be in his own life without every smell, wound, or bodily wave of nausea dragging him back there again.
